Type a word or a few lines in Latin or Hangul, pick a typeface and a colour, and press Generate until a growth feels right. Copy it into Figma as SVG, or record it growing.

Rhizoma Smoke is a type family and growth engine by the Sativus Gourd atelier, built on Rhizoma, Dabin Kim’s growing type system for the letters of IM Fell English. It adds Hangul, seeds that bring any growth back, smoke that climbs out of the letter, roots that join across letters and lines, and a current for SG Drag. Eight faces came out of it, with SG Smoke at the centre, and all eight install as fonts.

02Borderless connectionRoots that join across letters and lines.
“Any point of a rhizome can be connected to anything other, and must be.”

In A Thousand Plateaus, Deleuze and Guattari set two kinds of growth against each other. A tree grows from one root, so every branch traces back to a single origin. A rhizome has no centre: any part can connect to any other.

“A rhizome has no beginning or end; it is always in the middle, between things, interbeing, intermezzo.”

Rhizoma is named after the rhizome, but each of its roots grows like a tree: from one point to one tip, passing through other roots without meeting them. Rhizoma Smoke lets them connect. In SG Smoke Plume, SG Drag and SG Tangle, a root that comes near another letter, line or root joins it, so a word grows as one body and two lines as one field. SG Drag adds a current, so neighbouring roots travel together, braid and part, the way ink moves in water.

03Constant expansionRoots cross the space between lines and join the line above.

Set lines under each other and the growth crosses the gap between them. Smoke from the lower line climbs into the one above and fuses with it; a current carries roots across both; a tangle makes one mat of the whole paragraph. The text here is the last line of Voltaire’s Candide, which gave the tool its heading.

04How a letter growsRhizoma, the growing type system, step by step.

Rhizoma is a browser tool by the graphic designer Dabin Kim, shared on GitHub under a Creative Commons licence. Kim calls it “a growing type system.” It samples points inside each letter of IM Fell English, lets a few of them sprout, walks each root forward in small random turns, lets roots branch, and merges the roots with the letter into one outline that saves as a font or a vector file.

Rhizoma Smoke keeps that sequence. SG Rhizoma V2, in the tool above, runs the original engine at its default settings, so the method and the SG faces can be compared on the same text. SG Smoke stays closest to it: the same sampling and the same walk, with a seed, a taper and smoke that climbs. The other faces change where a root starts, how it moves and whether it meets anything. In SG Root, below, roots start on the outline and leave along its outward normal, so they grow out of the letter instead of across it.

IM Fell English is Igino Marini’s digitisation of the Fell Types, the founts Bishop John Fell left to Oxford in 1686. Type historians place the Fell Types between the Dutch old styles and William Caslon. Marini kept the uneven edges and ink spread of the printed originals, which is why the letter already looks grown.

05What changed in the engineWhat Rhizoma Smoke adds to Rhizoma v.01.

The engine keeps Rhizoma’s method: points in a letter sprout, each root walks forward in small turns and branches, and the roots and the letter merge into one outline. The additions sit on top of that method.

06Hangul / 한글Korean grown from Song Myung, in seven of the eight SG fonts.

For an atelier that sets Korean as often as English, Hangul was the first addition. Rhizoma Smoke reads two typefaces as one stack: Latin from IM Fell English and Hangul from Song Myung. Song Myung is an open Myeongjo, the Korean serif tradition, by the Song Myung Project. Both are under the SIL Open Font License. A syllable block holds far more ink than a Latin letter, so the fonts and the engine faces sprout Hangul at 0.45 of the Latin rate, and a Korean line grows about as densely as an English one. SG Smoke in the tool keeps the original rate, as it keeps every other setting. Every SG font except SG Tangle carries the 2,350 syllables of KS X 1001 and 51 jamo beside its Latin.

Hangul’s distinctions are small. One short stroke separates ㅏ from ㅑ, and a tick on top turns ㅈ into ㅊ. A root that leaves a stem in the wrong place can read as a stroke. The lower sprout rate is the first guard: fewer roots per syllable leaves fewer chances to land on a stem. The second is direction. In SG Smoke Plume and SG Smoke Flame, roots sprout only from edges that face upward and then rise, so no root starts on the side of a vertical stem, where ㅏ would turn into ㅑ and ㅓ into ㅕ.

The third is a guard in SG Root, the face that puts the most roots on a syllable. Once a line has grown, it takes out any Hangul root that leaves its syllable sideways, where the tick of ㅏ or ㅓ sits, and any root whose part outside the letter is short and nearly straight, the tick that turns ㅡ into ㅗ or ㅈ into ㅊ. Every other root stays where it grew, Latin is untouched, and the SG Root font carries the same guard.

Special thanks to Dabin Kim

Rhizoma Smoke is built upon Rhizoma, the growing type system Dabin Kim released openly under a CC BY-SA 4.0 licence. The engine supplies the method every face on this page depends on: points sampled inside the letterform, a share of them sprouting, and each root walked forward in small random turns and allowed to branch.

The SG Rhizoma Smoke additions extend beyond that method: Hangul, reproducible seeds, roots seeded on the outline, roots that join, directional fields, roots drawn as smooth curves, and fonts that set as running text. SG Smoke stays closest to the original model and changes only direction, taper, turbulence and how smoothly each root is drawn. SG Rhizoma V2 is the original engine at its default settings, with seeds, Hangul, and a font that installs with kerning and ligatures.
